Methodologies: CIMT ultrasound + PWMH MRI volumetry, logistic regression, ROC/AUC DeLong. Achievable Outcomes: a validated combined vascular-imaging index for PD-MCI risk stratification.
Journal: Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment 2025;21:2595-2602 - Dove Medical Press

Modality: EEG - resting-state spectral power, delta/alpha ratio, functional connectivity, and graph-theoretical network (small-world) metrics
Method_Architecture: Baseline resting-state EEG (spectral power, delta/alpha ratio, functional connectivity, small-world graph metrics) comparing biomarker-high-risk MCI who stayed stable (sMCI-resilient) vs converters (cMCI) vs healthy controls after 36 months (INTERCEPTOR).
Best_Metric: Group EEG differences: converters show frontal delta+/posterior alpha-/elevated delta-alpha ratio; resilient show stronger alpha connectivity + higher alpha-2 small-world index (no AUC)
Dataset: INTERCEPTOR project (Italian multi-centre MCI cohort)
Key_Novelty: EEG efficient-alpha-network signatures mark resilient (stable) high-risk MCI vs converters
Primary_Limitation: Observational, modest subgroups; resilience defined at 36 months; associational (no classifier/AUC)
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether the EEG resilience signature predicts (not just correlates with) long-term stability. Applications: EEG-based identification of resilient vs at-risk MCI for triage. Methodologies: resting EEG spectral/connectivity/small-world analysis across resilient/converter/control groups. Achievable Outcomes: a validated EEG resilience marker complementing structural/metabolic risk biomarkers.
Journal: Alzheimer's & Dementia: Translational Research & Clinical Interventions 2025;11:e70194 - Wiley on behalf of the Alzheimer's Association

Modality: FDG-PET (regional brain glucose metabolism) with causal modeling and deep learning
Method_Architecture: Structural causal modeling to identify FDG-PET regions causally influencing MMSE and FAQ; FDG CogNet deep-learning predictor with feature-wise attention; prediction of MMSE and FAQ (R-squared); ADNI CN/MCI/AD.
Best_Metric: R-squared 0.90 (MMSE) and 0.94 (FAQ) for FDG CogNet using causally-selected regions; cerebellar compensation in MCI diminishing in AD (no AUC)
Dataset: ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative)
Key_Novelty: Causal-DL FDG-PET (FDG CogNet) predicts MMSE R2 0.90 / FAQ 0.94 using causally-selected regions
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional ADNI-only; causal assumptions unverifiable; validation scheme underspecified (overfitting risk)
Open_Problems: Open Problems: validity/robustness of causal assumptions and generalisation beyond ADNI. Applications: interpretable FDG-PET-based cognition/function prediction and region-targeted intervention. Methodologies: structural causal modeling + FDG CogNet deep learning with feature-wise attention. Achievable Outcomes: a validated causal-region attention-based FDG-PET predictor of cognitive/functional decline.

Modality: Structural MRI (T1 hippocampal volumetry + T2 visual SRLM / hippocampal-atrophy scoring)
Method_Architecture: T1-weighted hippocampal volume segmentation; T2-weighted visual hippocampal atrophy and semi-quantitative SRLM integrity scoring; amyloid-stratified group comparisons across the AD continuum; correlations with cognition.
Best_Metric: Group SRLM/atrophy/volume differences (SRLM lower already in CU A+; reduced in MCI A+/AD A+); significant hippocampus-cognition correlations (no AUC)
Dataset: ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) - amyloid-stratified subset
Key_Novelty: Visual SRLM hippocampal-layer integrity declines early across the amyloid-stratified AD continuum
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional across-group trajectory; very small AD group (n=14); semi-quantitative rating variability
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether SRLM decline predicts conversion longitudinally and its quantitative automation. Applications: routine-T2 visual SRLM scoring for early AD detection. Methodologies: T1 hippocampal volumetry + T2 visual SRLM/atrophy scoring across an amyloid-stratified continuum. Achievable Outcomes: a validated early SRLM marker for clinical medial-temporal assessment.

Modality: EEG - quantitative EEG (broad-band power spectra, connectivity, complexity), resting eyes-closed
Method_Architecture: Eyes-closed resting qEEG features (power spectra, connectivity, complexity); machine-learning classifiers with feature-selection pipeline; trained on 88 SCI with 5-7 year follow-up; validated on two independent external cohorts.
Best_Metric: Prediction accuracy >80%, AUC 0.90 (SCI-to-MCI/dementia progression); robust across two external cohorts
Dataset: BrainScope-derived SCI cohort (n=88, 5-7 yr follow-up) + two independent external validation cohorts
Key_Novelty: qEEG ML biomarker predicts SCI->MCI/dementia (AUC 0.90); validated on 2 external cohorts
Primary_Limitation: Small derivation cohort (88); limited external-cohort detail; SCI heterogeneity; commercial context needs replication
Open_Problems: Open Problems: generalisation across devices/populations and comparison with plasma markers. Applications: earliest-stage (SCI) risk screening, monitoring, and trial enrichment. Methodologies: resting qEEG (power/connectivity/complexity) + ML classifiers with feature selection and external validation. Achievable Outcomes: a deployable externally-validated EEG biomarker for pre-MCI risk.

Modality: EEG - aperiodic (non-oscillatory) component (exponent/offset) and spectral power ratio from prefrontal two-channel resting EEG
Method_Architecture: Parameterized spectral estimation of aperiodic EEG (exponent, offset) and spectral power ratio from 5-min prefrontal two-channel resting EEG; SNSB and MMSE cognition; independent t-tests and generalized linear models testing APOE e4 x cognitive-state main and interaction effects.
Best_Metric: Significant APOE e4 x cognitive-state interactions in aperiodic exponent and SPR (carrier aMCI: heightened aperiodic activity, reduced SPR vs naMCI); no AUC
Dataset: GARD (Gwangju Alzheimer's and Related Dementia) cohort, Republic of Korea
Key_Novelty: Aperiodic EEG exponent/SPR x APOE4 interaction distinguishes aMCI from naMCI (GARD, N=1172)
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional; two-channel prefrontal montage; interaction patterns not a validated classifier; single-cohort
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether aperiodic-APOE signatures predict conversion longitudinally. Applications: aetiology-aware MCI subtype stratification using low-cost two-channel EEG plus genotype. Methodologies: parameterized spectral estimation (aperiodic exponent/offset, SPR) with GLM interaction analysis. Achievable Outcomes: a validated aperiodic-EEG-plus-APOE marker for MCI subtype and risk.
Journal: Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience 2026;17:1675330 - Frontiers Media

Modality: Neuropsychological testing / driving-behaviour outcomes (simulator and on-road) - review
Method_Architecture: Integrative literature review (MEDLINE/EMBASE/SCOPUS 2001-2020); eligibility screening (404->17); qualitative synthesis of cognitive domains associated with simulator/on-road driving outcomes in MCI/AD.
Best_Metric: Qualitative: attention, processing speed, executive function, visuospatial skills most linked to unsafe driving (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (integrative review; 17 included studies)
Key_Novelty: Review: attention/processing-speed/executive/visuospatial declines mark unsafe driving in MCI/AD
Primary_Limitation: Integrative (non-quantitative) review; heterogeneous, small, cross-culturally limited studies
Open_Problems: Open Problems: lack of standardised cross-cultural driving-fitness assessment for MCI/AD. Applications: domain-targeted neuropsychological screening for driving fitness. Methodologies: integrative review of simulator/on-road studies. Achievable Outcomes: an evidence-based cognitive-domain screening battery for fitness to drive.

Modality: Driving-behaviour assessment (standardized on-road performance) with neuropsychological testing and driver self-assessment
Method_Architecture: Standardized on-road driving assessment; neuropsychological testing; validity-of-self-assessment (VSA) index; hierarchical regression (age/sex then VSA); correlation analyses.
Best_Metric: On-road performance explained variance: age+sex adj R2 0.320 -> +VSA adj R2 0.639 (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house prospective cohort - Evangelisches Klinikum Bethel / Bielefeld University, Germany
Key_Novelty: Validity of self-assessment predicts on-road driving beyond age/sex in MCI (R2 0.32->0.64)
Primary_Limitation: Modest single-centre sample; observational (prediction not causation); instrument/culture specificity
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether improving self-assessment calibration reduces crash risk. Applications: VSA-based screening and feedback for older/MCI driver safety. Methodologies: standardized on-road assessment + neuropsychology + self-ratings with hierarchical regression. Achievable Outcomes: a validated VSA measure integrated into fitness-to-drive evaluation.

Modality: Multi-omics / molecular - diet-quality indices + gut-microbiota (16S) + serum microRNA expression
Method_Architecture: Diet-quality indices (CDGI-2018, E-DII, HLS); 16S gut-microbiota profiling; serum miRNA expression; logistic regression with ROC; relative-risk associations for MCI. EMCOA Chinese cohort.
Best_Metric: Combined diet+microbiota+miRNA signature AUC 0.91 (MCI vs healthy); diet-risk (CDGI RR 0.75, HLS RR 0.54, E-DII RR 1.46)
Dataset: EMCOA study (Chinese cohort; ChiCTR-OOC-17011882)
Key_Novelty: Diet+microbiota+miRNA combined signature distinguishes MCI (AUC 0.91); better diet lowers MCI risk
Primary_Limitation: Observational/associational; small microbiota+miRNA subset; region-specific; internal AUC only
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether diet-microbiota-miRNA links are causal/mediating and generalise. Applications: diet-based MCI prevention and a combinatorial biomarker. Methodologies: diet indices, 16S microbiota, serum miRNA, logistic-regression/ROC signature. Achievable Outcomes: an externally validated combined biomarker and diet-intervention target for MCI.
Journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2021;114:429-440 - ASN / Elsevier

Modality: Nutritional intervention (whey protein powder rich in MFGM, taurine, B vitamins) with cognitive-test outcomes
Method_Architecture: 12-month 1:1 randomized controlled trial (whey protein 15 g/d vs placebo); MoCA primary outcome; secondary cognitive subdomains (DSST) and body composition; intention-to-treat, modified-ITT, per-protocol analyses.
Best_Metric: MoCA between-group difference 1.81 (95% CI 0.32-3.30) at 12 mo (whey 3.23 vs control 1.42); DSST diff 2.72 (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house randomized controlled trial - Wuhan University, China (ChiCTR2200062705)
Key_Novelty: 12-mo whey-protein (MFGM/taurine/B-vitamin) RCT improves MoCA in MCI (between-group +1.81)
Primary_Limitation: Modest single-region sample; 1-year follow-up; multi-ingredient formulation; cognition (not conversion) endpoint
Open_Problems: Open Problems: which component drives the effect and whether benefits persist/delay conversion. Applications: nutritional supplementation for cognitive maintenance in MCI. Methodologies: 12-month double-arm RCT with MoCA primary and ITT analysis. Achievable Outcomes: a validated dietary intervention shown to slow cognitive decline in MCI.
Journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2025;121:256-264 - ASN / Elsevier

Modality: Clinical/hematological marker (blood hemoglobin) with MoCA cognitive assessment (longitudinal cohort)
Method_Architecture: Observational analysis of the 3-year DO-HEALTH RCT; MoCA at 0/12/24/36 mo (MCI=MoCA<26 at two consecutive points); baseline hemoglobin quintiles and anemia exposures; logistic regression via generalized estimating equations with multivariable adjustment.
Best_Metric: MCI odds by hemoglobin quintile vs lowest: Q2 OR 0.66, Q3 0.61, Q4 0.56, Q5 0.64 (all significant); anemia null (no AUC)
Dataset: DO-HEALTH trial (European community-dwelling older adults; NCT01745263)
Key_Novelty: Higher baseline hemoglobin (>=130 g/L) linked to 34-44% lower MCI odds over 3y (DO-HEALTH)
Primary_Limitation: Observational secondary analysis; residual confounding; screening-based MCI definition; generally-healthy cohort
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether the hemoglobin-MCI link is causal and its mechanism. Applications: hemoglobin as a routine marker in cognitive-risk assessment. Methodologies: longitudinal MoCA-defined MCI with hemoglobin-quintile GEE logistic regression. Achievable Outcomes: a validated modifiable hematological risk marker for MCI.
Journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (2025) - ASN / Elsevier

Modality: Multicomponent exercise intervention (aerobic + endurance + balance + flexibility) with cognitive/physical/ADL outcomes - meta-analysis
Method_Architecture: PROSPERO-registered systematic review of RCTs (PubMed/Embase/Web of Science/Cochrane through May 2022); Cochrane risk-of-bias; random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges g, 95% CI); Egger/trim-and-fill/leave-one-out sensitivity analyses.
Best_Metric: MCI global cognition Hedges g=0.978 (95% CI 0.298-1.659); executive function g=0.448; dementia effects g 0.34-1.13 (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (meta-analysis of 21 RCTs; PROSPERO CRD42022324641)
Key_Novelty: Meta-analysis: multicomponent exercise improves cognition & executive function in MCI/dementia
Primary_Limitation: Modest RCT count (21); heterogeneous protocols; wide CI on MCI global-cognition effect; publication-bias risk
Open_Problems: Open Problems: optimal exercise dose/composition and durability of cognitive benefit. Applications: exercise prescription for cognitive/functional maintenance in MCI/dementia. Methodologies: PROSPERO-registered systematic review + random-effects meta-analysis. Achievable Outcomes: evidence-based multicomponent-exercise guidelines for MCI/dementia.
Journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation 2023;104:2092-2108 - ACRM / Elsevier

Modality: Gait / motor assessment (single-task and dual-task gait tests) for cognitive screening
Method_Architecture: Single-task and dual-task (counting backwards, serial subtractions of 7, naming animals) gait tests; binary logistic regression; ROC/AUC model selection; external validation with ROC and calibration curves (education-adjusted).
Best_Metric: External-validation AUC 0.913 (dual-task serial-subtraction-7 gait model); derivation AUC 0.906 / accuracy 0.831
Dataset: In-house community cohort - Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China (derivation + external validation)
Key_Novelty: Dual-task gait (serial-subtraction-7) diagnostic model detects MCI, externally validated AUC 0.913
Primary_Limitation: Modest single-region samples; case-control design; not tested in consecutive screening populations
Open_Problems: Open Problems: real-world screening performance in unselected populations. Applications: community/primary-care gait-based MCI screening. Methodologies: single- vs dual-task gait tests, logistic regression, ROC/AUC, external validation with calibration. Achievable Outcomes: a deployable validated dual-task gait screening tool for MCI.
Journal: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation 2024;105:930-938 - ACRM / Elsevier

Modality: Clinical / neuropsychiatric - Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPS) with longitudinal cognitive and conversion outcomes
Method_Architecture: Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI); latent class analysis of NPS patterns; linear mixed models of 5-year cognitive change; Cox proportional-hazards models for MCI-to-AD conversion adjusted for age, sex, education, global cognition, APOE e4. ADNI.
Best_Metric: MCI-to-AD conversion HR vs no-NPS: apathy/affective 1.39 (95% CI 1.10-1.76), complex 2.03 (1.33-3.10); accelerated decline in apathy/affective class (no AUC)
Dataset: ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative)
Key_Novelty: Latent NPS classes predict MCI-to-AD conversion (HR up to 2.03) and faster cognitive decline (ADNI)
Primary_Limitation: Observational ADNI; single-baseline NPS classification; no biological markers; small complex-NPS group
Open_Problems: Open Problems: neurobiological mechanisms underlying NPS classes and their stability. Applications: NPS-phenotype-based prognostic stratification in MCI. Methodologies: latent class analysis of NPI, linear mixed models, Cox conversion modelling. Achievable Outcomes: a validated NPS-phenotype prognostic tool linked to biological mechanisms.

Modality: Cognitive/behavioural - episodic memory (detail vs gist) testing under unisensory/multisensory encoding, with medial-temporal correlates
Method_Architecture: Detail and gist episodic-memory tests with 14-day retrieval; unisensory (audio) vs multisensory (audiovisual) encoding; ANCOVA (age/sex/education); correlations between behavioural performance and medial-temporal brain variables.
Best_Metric: Group memory differences (aMCI worse on detail and gist; longer-lasting gist gap); multisensory encoding reduces gaps esp. gist (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house cohort - National Taiwan University / NTU Hospital, Taiwan
Key_Novelty: Gist memory shows a longer-lasting aMCI deficit than detail; multisensory encoding rescues gist
Primary_Limitation: Modest single-centre sample; short 14-day follow-up; behavioural (no conversion outcome); correlational brain links
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether gist deficits and multisensory rescue predict conversion, and their neural basis. Applications: gist-sensitive memory assessment and multisensory-encoding strategies for aMCI. Methodologies: detail/gist memory tests over 14 days, encoding manipulation, ANCOVA, brain-behaviour correlation. Achievable Outcomes: encoding-based rehabilitation and refined memory markers for aMCI.

Modality: Cognitive/behavioural with eye tracking - visual working-memory binding and overt attention during object-scene integration
Method_Architecture: Eye-tracking change-detection task with naturalistic scenes; manipulation of object saliency and semantic consistency; overt-attention measures (fixation latency/duration); group comparison across younger adults, healthy older adults, and MCI.
Best_Metric: Change-detection accuracy by group/condition; semantic-inconsistency prioritisation and fixation-duration benefits across all groups; VWM binding preserved in MCI (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house cohort - Sapienza University of Rome / IRCCS Fondazione Santa Lucia, Italy
Sample_N_Approx: 95 (younger adults / healthy older adults / MCI; MCI n=30 accuracy / 21 eye-movement analysis)
Key_Novelty: VWM object-scene binding & attention preserved in MCI (challenges generalized-impairment view)
Primary_Limitation: Experimental (non-diagnostic); single-centre, cross-sectional; MCI subtype not resolved; MCI raw detection accuracy still lower than controls
Open_Problems: Open Problems: whether preserved binding holds in adequately powered subtype-resolved MCI samples. Applications: attention/compensation-informed cognitive assessment and rehabilitation. Methodologies: eye-tracking change detection with saliency/semantic manipulation. Achievable Outcomes: a validated account of which VWM/attention processes are spared vs impaired in MCI.

Modality: Environmental-exposure epidemiology - air pollution (PM2.5/PM/NO2/NOx/CO/SO2), occupational (shift work), chronic noise, ELF magnetic fields, greenness - umbrella review
Method_Architecture: Umbrella review (PRISMA/JBI); multi-level random-effects meta-analysis of risk ratios with study-overlap adjustment; narrative synthesis for non-poolable exposures; secondary analy
Best_Metric: 9 exposures raise all-cause dementia risk (PM2.5/PM/NO2/NOx/CO/shift+night-shift work/chronic noise/ELF-MF); greenness protective (pooled risk ratios; no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (umbrella review; 19 reviews / 37 meta-analyses; PROSPERO CRD42021291607)
Key_Novelty: Umbrella review pooling environmental dementia risks; documents near-absent MCI-specific evidence
Primary_Limitation: Observational review-level evidence; overlap across reviews; exposure-measurement heterogeneity; English-only; and no systematic review reporting on MCI outcomes.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether environmental exposures predict MCI (not just dementia); dose-response and phenotype-specific effects. - **Applications:** Air-quality standards, occupational (shift-work) and neighbourhood (greenness, noise) public-health interventions. - **Methodologies:** Umbrella review; multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with overlap adjustment; narrative synthesis. - **Achievable outcomes:** Quantified, policy-relevant environmental risk estimates and a defined MCI evidence gap.

Modality: Dance intervention (physical-cognitive-social) with cognitive / physical-function / depression / quality-of-life outcomes - meta-analysis
Method_Architecture: Seven-database systematic search; RCT inclusion; risk-of-bias assessment; random-effects meta-analysis of SMDs across global cognition, cognitive domains, physical function, depres
Best_Metric: Global cognition SMD 0.54; QoL 0.93; physical function 0.55; memory 0.33 / visuospatial 0.42 / language 0.39 (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs; PROSPERO CRD42020173659)
Sample_N_Approx: 8 studies (N range 31-201; 455 pooled for global cognition)
Key_Novelty: MCI meta-analysis: dance improves cognition, physical function and quality of life
Primary_Limitation: Few RCTs (8), modest pooled samples, high heterogeneity, short follow-ups, and sparse neuroimaging/biomarker outcomes.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Mechanisms (neuroplasticity), optimal dance type/dose, durability of effects, and effect on progression. - **Applications:** Community and clinical dance programmes for older adults with MCI. - **Methodologies:** Systematic review + random-effects meta-analysis of RCTs; subgroup analysis by instrument. - **Achievable outcomes:** Evidence-based, scalable non-pharmacological cognitive-and-physical intervention.

Modality: Empowerment-based educative psycho-behavioural program - neuropsychiatric-symptom / cognition / quality-of-life outcomes (mixed-methods RCT)
Method_Architecture: Single-blinded RCT with descriptive qualitative follow-up; 13-week empowerment-based educative psycho-behavioural program vs generic health education; standardised neuropsychiatric
Best_Metric: GEE: overall NPS beta -1.49 (p .044); subjective memory -1.97 (p .003); anxiety -0.53 (p .009); apathy 2.14 (p .018) (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house RCT cohort - five social facilities, Hong Kong (HKUCTR-2915)
Key_Novelty: Empowerment psycho-behavioural RCT targeting neuropsychiatric symptoms in MCI
Primary_Limitation: Single-region, predominantly female, single-blinded, short follow-up; some effects delayed; generalisability uncertain.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Durability of effects, mechanism, and whether reducing neuropsychiatric symptoms slows conversion. - **Applications:** Community nursing programs targeting neuropsychiatric symptoms in MCI. - **Methodologies:** Explanatory sequential mixed methods; single-blinded RCT; GEE; qualitative interviews. - **Achievable outcomes:** A deliverable empowerment-based program improving mood and cognition in MCI.

Modality: Barriers/motivators to physical-activity participation in MCI/dementia - umbrella review (TDF/BCT mapping)
Method_Architecture: Seven-database umbrella review; dual quality appraisal (MetaQAT + AMSTAR); GRADE-CERQual confidence grading; Theoretical Domains Framework mapping; Behaviour Change Technique-based
Best_Metric: 31 barrier/motivator factors; strongest = resources/material resources, social support, perceived competence; 6 implementation strategies (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (umbrella review; 14 reviews / >219 primary studies; PROSPERO CRD42022371535)
Key_Novelty: Theory-mapped umbrella review of physical-activity barriers/motivators in MCI/dementia
Primary_Limitation: Variable review quality; overlapping primary studies; many factors of moderate/low confidence; interpretive strategy mapping.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Which strategies actually raise participation and adherence; under-evidenced determinants. - **Applications:** Designing tailored, supported physical-activity programs for MCI/dementia. - **Methodologies:** JBI umbrella review; MetaQAT/AMSTAR appraisal; GRADE-CERQual; TDF/BCT mapping. - **Achievable outcomes:** Theory-based, deliverable implementation strategies for physical-activity promotion.

Modality: Multimodal behavioural/digital - speech (audio) + facial expression (video) + text features for neuropsychiatric-symptom classification in MCI
Method_Architecture: Cross-sectional multimodal data collection (audio, video, text); open-source feature extraction; multiclass classification (random forest best); SHAP-based explainability; symptom
Best_Metric: F1 96.6% (weighted-avg, multiclass); Acc 87.4%; Prec 86.6%; Rec 87.6%
Dataset: In-house cohort - memory outpatient clinic, tertiary hospital, China (ChiCTR1900023892)
Key_Novelty: Multimodal speech+face+text random forest distinguishing depression, anxiety and apathy in MCI
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional, single-centre; internal-only model development; very high headline metrics risk overfitting; unclear external/multilingual generalisability.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** External/longitudinal validation; language and device generalisability; overfitting risk. - **Applications:** Remote, objective neuropsychiatric-symptom monitoring in MCI nursing care. - **Methodologies:** Multimodal (speech/facial/text) feature extraction; random-forest multiclass classification; SHAP explainability. - **Achievable outcomes:** An objective screening/monitoring tool for depression, anxiety, and apathy in MCI.

Modality: Multicomponent (physical + motor) exercise - global-cognition and cognitive-subdomain outcomes - meta-analysis
Method_Architecture: Six-database systematic search; RCT inclusion; Cochrane risk-of-bias; random-effects SMD meta-analysis across global cognition and subdomains; subgroup analysis, meta-regression, s
Best_Metric: Global cognition SMD 1.04 (0.53-1.55); cardio+motor combo SMD 1.06 (0.55-1.57); subdomain SMD 0.36-0.43 (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (meta-analysis of 20 RCTs; PROSPERO CRD42023400302)
Key_Novelty: Meta-analysis: multicomponent exercise improves cognitive subdomains; cardio+motor best
Primary_Limitation: Wide CIs and heterogeneity; motor component not subclassified; undetermined optimal dose/intensity; some subdomains based on few studies.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Optimal intensity/dose and detailed motor-component combinations; durability. - **Applications:** Evidence-based multicomponent exercise prescriptions for MCI. - **Methodologies:** Systematic review + random-effects meta-analysis; subgroup/meta-regression/sensitivity analyses. - **Achievable outcomes:** Domain-specific, component-optimised exercise programs for MCI.

Modality: Trans-theoretical-model health education - knowledge / behavioural-stage / adherence / cognition / dexterity outcomes (RCT)
Method_Architecture: Assessor-blinded two-arm RCT; TTM-based education (8 weeks + 12 weeks unsupervised) vs standard education; assessments at baseline/8/20 weeks; group-level GEE and individual-level
Best_Metric: GEE 20-wk: adherence beta 10.74; global cognition 2.42; disease knowledge 1.78; behavioural stage 1.72 (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house RCT cohort - community-dwelling older adults, Huzhou, China (ChiCTR1900028351)
Key_Novelty: Trans-theoretical-model education in MCI with clinically-significant-change analysis
Primary_Limitation: Single-city, modest sample; wait-list control; individual-level effects smaller than group averages; no benefit for depression/sleep.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Mechanisms of cognition/behaviour enhancement; durability; why individual-level effects are smaller. - **Applications:** Community health-education programs improving self-management in MCI. - **Methodologies:** Two-arm assessor-blinded RCT; GEE; reliable and clinically significant change analysis. - **Achievable outcomes:** A theory-based education program with standardised clinical-significance benchmarks.

Modality: Reminiscence-therapy delivery formats (digital/individual/group) - cognition / depression / quality-of-life / adherence outcomes - network meta-analysis
Method_Architecture: Nine-database systematic search; RCT inclusion; frequentist network meta-analysis; SUCRA ranking of delivery formats; node-splitting for inconsistency.
Best_Metric: Digital SUCRA 93.6% (cognition) / 94.9% (depression); individual 98.3% (QoL); group 95.6% (adherence) (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (network meta-analysis of 53 RCTs / 4582 participants; PROSPERO CRD42024530754)
Key_Novelty: Network meta-analysis ranking reminiscence-therapy delivery formats per outcome in dementia/MCI
Primary_Limitation: Transitivity/sparse-network assumptions; large effects with wide CIs; combined dementia+MCI populations; varying format definitions.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** MCI-specific format effects; transitivity and sparse-network robustness; standard format definitions. - **Applications:** Format-tailored reminiscence-therapy programs in community and institutional care. - **Methodologies:** Systematic review + frequentist network meta-analysis; SUCRA ranking; node-splitting. - **Achievable outcomes:** Outcome-specific delivery-format recommendations for reminiscence therapy.

Modality: Qualitative meta-synthesis of lived experience of MCI (cognitive / psychological / social dimensions); no biomarker or device modality
Method_Architecture: Six-database systematic search; meta-synthesis of qualitative studies; thematic analysis into third-order constructs; integration with stress-coping and psychological-flexibility t
Best_Metric: Qualitative - 3 themes integrated into the Dynamic Stress-Response for Cognitive Decline Model (no numeric metric; no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (meta-synthesis of 20 qualitative studies; PROSPERO CRD42023471772)
Key_Novelty: Dynamic Stress-Response for Cognitive Decline Model from MCI lived-experience meta-synthesis
Primary_Limitation: Interpretive qualitative evidence; conceptual model not yet empirically validated; cultural variability; dependence on primary-study quality.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Empirical validation of the model; cross-cultural generalisability; linking coping to outcomes. - **Applications:** Person-centred psychosocial interventions supporting adaptive coping in MCI. - **Methodologies:** Qualitative meta-synthesis; thematic analysis to third-order constructs; theory integration. - **Achievable outcomes:** A validated biopsychosocial coping framework informing MCI support.

Modality: Neuromodulation (gamma-tACS vs tDCS over DLPFC) with quantitative EEG (sLORETA) and cognitive (Stroop/TMT) outcomes
Method_Architecture: Sham-controlled, double-blinded, counterbalanced repeated-measures crossover; 40 Hz gamma-tACS and tDCS at 2 mA over DLPFC for 30 min; Stroop and Trail-Making Test; quantitative EE
Best_Metric: Gamma-tACS > tDCS on Stroop-color (p .044) and > sham (p .010); TMT-B > sham (p .021); tDCS not different from sham (no AUC)
Dataset: In-house cohort - Chuncheon Sacred Heart Hospital / Hallym University, Republic of Korea
Key_Novelty: First direct tACS-vs-tDCS comparison in MCI; gamma-tACS beats tDCS via increased beta
Primary_Limitation: Very small n (20); single-session, immediate outcomes only; untested durability/clinical relevance; crossover with short washout.

Modality: Clinical/population - neuropsychological domain-based MCI subtyping with longitudinal MMSE/FAQ trajectories (ADNI cohort)

Method_Architecture: Randomised double-blind sham-controlled crossover trial, 30 sessions over 10 weeks per phase with 4-week washout; Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Cohen's d, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
Best_Metric: MoCA active-rTMS intragroup Cohen's d (SMD) 1.61 (23.2 +/- 1.5 to 25.7 +/- 1.4, p = 0.011); MoCA intergroup p = 0.005 at start of phase 2, d 1.32 in the other arm (no AUC)
Dataset: No public dataset - single-centre Mexican clinical trial sample from the Nervous System Clinic, Faculty of Medicine, Autonomous University of Queretaro, and the Mental Health Center of the State of Queretaro (CESAM); registered NCT03906903
Sample_N_Approx: 22 (11 Group A SG-AG / 11 Group B AG-SG; 13 women, 9 men; mean age 66.36 +/- 5.12 years); 80 screened, 24 randomised, 2 withdrawals

Heavy selection (80 screened but only 24 randomised, largely for comorbidity and rTMS contraindications) left a medically stable, highly educated single-centre Mexican retiree sample; no formal crossover analysis of period or carryover terms was performed even though the sham phases also produced gains; previous occupational and nutritional status were not recorded; the ST-hits measure described in the methods is never reported; and the Table 1 footnote and Section 3 assign several intragroup p values to opposite groups.

Modality: Meta-analytic synthesis of subjective sleep instruments (PSQI, Athens Insomnia Scale, ESS, NPI-12/NPI-Q, HAMD) plus actigraphy and polysomnography; no neuroimaging
Method_Architecture: PRISMA/MOOSE systematic review with STATA 'metaprop' inverse-variance random-effects pooling of proportions; I2 heterogeneity, subgroup analysis, meta-regression, trim-and-fill
Best_Metric: Pooled subjective sleep-disturbance prevalence 35.8% (95% CI 31.9-39.7, I2 = 98.03%, 44 studies); objective 46.3% (36.3-56.3, 6 studies) (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (meta-analysis of 52 observational MCI studies from 24 countries; six databases searched from inception to 20 January 2024)
Sample_N_Approx: 52 studies / 25,915 participants included; 25,443 participants across the 44 subjective-arm studies pooled; 6 studies / 201 individuals in the objective arm
Key_Novelty: First global meta-analysis of subjective and objective sleep-disturbance prevalence in MCI
Primary_Limitation: The objective prevalence of 46.3% derives from only 6 studies and 201 individuals, with assessment durations of one night to one week and only three poolable indicators (TST, WASO, SE). The subjective estimate carries near-maximal heterogeneity (I2 = 98.03%) that persisted within every subgroup, and Egger's test indicated publication bias although trim-and-fill left the estimates unchanged. MCI criteria differed across studies (Petersen, DSM-5, CDR, ICD-10) and only 14 of 52 used CT or MRI; sleep-drug use, comorbidity and MCI duration were unavailable; no low-income countries were included.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Why self-report (49.4%) and informant rating (23.7%) diverge so far within the same condition; whether the SE >= 85% healthy-adult threshold is valid in MCI; why North America (19.1%) sits far below Europe (40.9%), Asia (39.4%) and Oceania (45.2%); why cohort designs (26.6%) yield lower estimates than cross-sectional (40.8%). - **Applications:** A global burden figure and prevalence map to guide screening policy and resource allocation; sleep monitoring as non-invasive early screening. - **Methodologies:** PRISMA/MOOSE six-database search, JBI appraisal, metaprop pooling.

Best_Metric: SMD 1.21 (95% CI 0.69-1.73) CCT2x vs control on global cognition; working memory 0.93 (0.44-1.42); episodic memory 0.87 (0.47-1.27); depressive symptoms -0.77 (-1.08 to -0.45) (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (network meta-analysis of 10 mobile-app cognitive-training RCTs; PubMed/Medline, EMBASE, Scopus, Cochrane Library to end of June 2024; PROSPERO CRD42024566476)
Sample_N_Approx: 10 RCTs; per-trial N 19 to 117 (Rozzini 59, Herrera 22, Singh 100, Gooding 74, Djabelkhir 19, Kwan 33, Robert 43, Callisaya 93, Harvey 117, Schmitter 29); pooled participant total not reported in source
Key_Novelty: Network meta-analysis ranking seven interventions and control in MCI/dementia mobile-app RCTs
Primary_Limitation: The network rests on only 10 small RCTs (per-trial N 19 to 117, durations 4 to 52 weeks) that are almost entirely Western, use heterogeneous and operationally defined CCT protocols and outcome scales, leaving several comparisons on a single trial; the authors state this heterogeneity compromises the validity of their consistency claim. MCI and dementia were pooled despite differing prognoses and some cohorts were not strictly MCI. Reporting is internally inconsistent - 89 full texts minus 70 exclusions leaves 19 yet 10 were included, and the CCT plus PRT ADL effect is opposite-signed to CCT.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether the CCT2x advantage is a true dose-response or greater engagement among less impaired users; whether effects persist beyond the 4 to 52 week trial windows; whether app training slows MCI-to-dementia progression; the opposite-signed CCT plus PRT ADL estimate. - **Applications:** Mobile cognitive-training apps in MCI/dementia care plans - CCT2x for cognition and mood, CCT for ADLs; low-cost home and community deployment. - **Methodologies:** PRISMA-NMA review; four-database search to June 2024; random-effects netmeta; node-splitting; SUCRA; Egger test; RoB 2.0.

Modality: Occupational responder cohort - SCID-5 psychiatric interview (PTSD, MDE), neuropsychological battery (HVLT, TMT-A/B, SDMT, COWA, BNT) plus CogState; no neuroimaging
Method_Architecture: Multivariable robust quasi-Poisson regression with Huber-White sandwich errors; Levin-type attributable fractions with 1000-resample bootstrap; FDR-controlled partial Spearman
Best_Metric: Comorbid PTSD/MDE adjusted RR 2.31 (95% CI 1.74-3.06, p < 0.001); PTSD RR 1.90, MDE RR 1.62; total PAF 11.7% (95% CI 6.1-18.1) (no AUC)
Dataset: FDNY World Trade Center-exposed responder cohort (WTC Health Program, Stony Brook University), collected November 2021 to December 2023
Sample_N_Approx: 337 (280 neither / 39 PTSD only / 6 MDE only / 12 comorbid PTSD and MDE; 153 with MCI), from 343 enrolled
Key_Novelty: Extends prior WTC-responder work with context-specific PAFs for PTSD, MDE and their comorbidity
Primary_Limitation: The cross-sectional design cannot establish whether PTSD and MDE precede, follow or co-occur with MCI, and with only 6 MDE-only cases the depression-without-PTSD estimate is uninformative; activities of daily living were never measured and there is no unexposed or non-FDNY comparison group, so the PAFs are valid only within this predominantly male, non-Latino White firefighter cohort.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Temporal ordering of PTSD, MDE and MCI is unresolved by a cross-sectional design; whether MDE without PTSD carries independent risk cannot be answered with 6 cases; the etiology of the >85% of MCI not attributable to psychiatric diagnosis (occupational toxins, particulate exposure, cumulative stress, inflammation) is open. - **Applications:** Occupational-health screening prioritising responders with both PTSD and MDE, positive screens triggering full neuropsychological assessment; PAFs bounding the achievable gain from psychiatric treatment. - **Methodologies:** SCID-5
Journal: Psychiatry Research, volume 355 (2026), article number 116827; Elsevier B.V.

Modality: Published observational cohorts - depression rating scales (GDS-15/30, CES-D, NPI, MADRS, HDRS, PHQ-8, EURO-D, BDI) plus Petersen/Winblad MCI criteria or MMSE/MoCA/CDR screens; no imaging
Method_Architecture: PRISMA systematic review; random-effects meta-analysis of proportions across 52 observational studies with Q/I-squared, leave-one-out, Egger's test, trim-and-fill and six subgroups
Best_Metric: Pooled StD prevalence 28.1% (95% CI 24.2%-32.0%, I-squared 98.4%, 52 studies); largest contrast hospital 36.2% (28.9-43.6) vs community 21.6% (18.0-25.1) (no AUC)
Dataset: No primary dataset - 52 published observational studies (2001-2024) of MCI cohorts from 17 countries across 6 continents; ten-database search to 27 March 2025; PROSPERO CRD420251020503
Sample_N_Approx: 52 studies, 29,321 older adults with MCI (29 community-based / 23 hospital-based studies; individual MCI sample sizes 21 to 8,004)
Key_Novelty: First meta-analysis of subthreshold-depression prevalence specifically in older adults with MCI
Primary_Limitation: The StD case definition was deliberately broad - 46 of 52 studies merely indicated depressive symptoms with no clinical assessment excluding MDD and only 6 applied DSM criteria - so the 28.1% pooled estimate merges non-equivalent constructs, instruments and cut-offs and carries I-squared = 98.4% heterogeneity that six prespecified subgroup analyses failed to resolve. Inclusion was restricted to English- and Chinese-language reports; Egger's test was significant (p = 0.040) yet trim-and-fill imputed nothing; subgroup claims rest on within-stratum heterogeneity p-values, not between-group tests.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether StD in MCI is one construct or several non-equivalent ones (DSM-ascertained 21.3% vs symptom-only 28.9%, both I-squared above 83%); why European estimates (34.5%) exceed Asian ones (20.1%); whether the age gradient above 60 is real or inflated by somatic-item overlap. - **Applications:** A 28.1% planning figure for StD burden in MCI services; brief geriatric depression screens in routine cognitive assessment; setting-specific expectations of about 36% hospital versus 22% community. - **Methodologies:** Ten-database PROSPERO search, JBI nine-item appraisal
Journal: Psychiatry Research, volume 357 (2026), article number 116922; Elsevier B.V.

Modality: Scalp EEG cognitive event-related potentials at or after 150 ms (N200, P300, N400, LPC, parietal effect, LPP, slow waves) tabulated with task and electrode montage, plus study-level demographics and MMSE; no primary neuroimaging
Method_Architecture: Narrative systematic review without meta-analysis; two-database Boolean search with four inclusion criteria and a categorised full-text exclusion audit; component-wise amplitude and latency tabulation; cross-study t-tests, one-way and mixed ANOVA with partial eta squared; majority/minority pattern synthesis for components with 3 or more studies
Best_Metric: Proportion of studies detecting a significant group difference - N400 amplitude 76 % (AD) and 67 % (MCI) vs P300 amplitude 60 % / 38 %, P300 latency 66 % / 41 %, N200 latency 50 % / 47 % and N200 amplitude 18 % / 22 %; largest self-computed statistic MMSE diagnostic vs control F(1,51) = 57.5, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.53 (no AUC)
Dataset: No primary dataset - synthesis of 100 published ERP studies (47 MCI, 47 AD, 6 APOE e4) retrieved from PsycINFO and PubMed, supplemented by the 42-study reference set of Gu and Zhang's 2017 MCI review; search cut-off not reported in source
Sample_N_Approx: 100 studies / 3,922 participants - 2,359 in MCI vs HC studies (47 studies), 1,445 in AD vs HC studies (47 studies), 118 in APOE e4 vs e4- studies (6 studies)
Key_Novelty: First systematic review of cognitive ERPs (>=150 ms) across MCI, AD and APOE e4 carriers
Primary_Limitation: Small, unbalanced and age-mismatched cells (AD mean 15.2, APOE mean 12 per group) plus near-absent contrast data and effect-size reporting preclude pooling, so all conclusions remain vote-counts of study percentages; the APOE e4 arm rests on 6 studies and 118 participants
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether N200 amplitude is genuinely insensitive in pathological aging or the 67 % (MCI), 82 % (AD) and 100 % (APOE) null rates reflect small unbalanced cells and passive oddball tasks; whether P300a and P300b behave differently, which no reviewed study allowed the authors to determine; whether the frontal N400 is functionally identical to the classical N400; whether ERP latency change precedes cognitive decline in e4 carriers, suggested by a single 3.5-year follow-up. - **Applications:** ERPs as an affordable MRI-alternative adjunct for early detection, differential diagnosis and progression tracking. - **Methodologies:** Two-database search with four inclusion criteria; component-wise amplitude/latency tabulation with montage; cross-study t-tests and ANOVAs; majority-versus-minority synthesis. - **Achievable outcomes:** Well-powered age-matched studies using complex executive and semantic tasks with lateral electrodes, routine effect-size reporting, and explicit sensitivity/specificity estimates
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 396 (2021), article number 112904; Elsevier B.V. (Review article; ISSN 0166-4328)

Modality: Meta-analytic synthesis of behavioural interval-timing task indices (absolute error, percent error, coefficient of variation, standard deviation, bisection point, Weber ratio) plus screening and neuropsychological instruments (MMSE, MoCA, MODA, RAVLT, CERAD, CAMCOG-R, Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing, TMT-A); no neuroimaging or electrophysiology
Method_Architecture: PRISMA systematic review with two multi-level random-effects meta-analyses (prospective, retrospective) of Hedges g nested within study, Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman inference, Q/tau-squared/I-squared, six-moderator meta-regression, AICc selection via glmulti, robust variance estimation (metafor in R)
Best_Metric: Pooled prospective-timing Hedges g = -0.49 (95% CI -0.76 to -0.23, z = -3.76, p < .001); AD g = -0.72, MCI g = -0.08 (p = .309) but fitted g = -0.41 under meta-regression; retrospective g = -0.29 (no AUC)
Dataset: Not applicable (synthesis of 12 published timing studies giving 14 independent samples and 80 effect sizes; PsycInfo, PubMed and Web of Science searched without date restriction to February 2020 plus reference-list hand-searching; extracted data at https://osf.io/k58zp/)
Sample_N_Approx: 562 (254 patients - 143 AD / 111 MCI - plus 308 healthy older controls; 12 studies / 14 independent samples / 80 effect sizes)
Key_Novelty: Meta-regression reveals an MCI timing deficit hidden by the random-effects model
Primary_Limitation: Only 12 underpowered studies; the null random-effects MCI result and the fitted meta-regression deficit disagree, leaving MCI timing unresolved.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether prospective timing is genuinely spared in MCI or the null random-effects result is an artefact of insensitive measures, few studies and a narrow age band - fitted g = -0.41 versus observed g = -0.08 is the crux; whether MCI subtypes differ in timing; why patient-control differences shrink with sample age; whether the direction of temporal bias differs, untested because absolute error was pooled; whether the deficit is attentional or mnemonic. - **Applications:** Low-cost timing tasks as behavioural indices of attentional and working-memory compromise in AD.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 410 (2021), article 113354; Elsevier B.V. (Review article)

Modality: 3.0 T resting-state fMRI (240 volumes) with sagittal MP-RAGE T1 and axial T2 lesion screening, parcellated into 116 x 116 AAL functional connectomes, plus MMSE/MDRS-2/AVLT-IR/DR/recognition and CDR battery
Method_Architecture: Connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM): covariate-adjusted mass-univariate edge selection at p < 0.05, positive and negative network-strength summation into linear regression, LOOCV with 1000-iteration permutation testing; ANOVA/chi-square group comparison
Best_Metric: r = 0.218 (Pearson, observed vs LOOCV-predicted AVLT-DR, negative network model, permutation p = 0.045); positive network r = 0.033 (p = 0.293), not significant (no AUC)
Dataset: Single-centre clinical cohort recruited by community health screening and newspaper advertisement, Department of Neurology, Affiliated ZhongDa Hospital, Southeast University, Nanjing, China; not a public dataset, no cohort name reported
Sample_N_Approx: 86 (33 CN / 26 SCD / 27 aMCI); 53 patients (26 SCD + 27 aMCI) entered the connectome-based predictive model
Key_Novelty: CPM predicts AVLT-DR episodic memory across SCD and aMCI; only the negative network works
Primary_Limitation: Weak, unreplicated effect: r = 0.218 at permutation p = 0.045 from LOOCV on 53 single-centre patients, with no held-out partition, no external validation and the 10-fold and leave-one-group-out numbers never printed.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Why the negative network predicted AVLT-DR while the positive network failed, when prior CPM work on intelligence and attention found the two comparable; whether this is a genuine dis-connectivity signature or compensatory prefrontal-temporal-parietal recruitment in aMCI but not SCD; whether an r = 0.218 model is stable in an independent cohort; whether it extends to cognitively normal elderly, who were scanned but excluded. - **Applications:** Individual-level, assessor-independent rs-fMRI readout of episodic memory for predementia staging.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 411 (2021), article 113387, Research report; Elsevier B.V.

Modality: EEG - 64-channel task-evoked electrophysiology; event-related spectral perturbation (theta 4-7 Hz ERS, alpha 8-12 Hz ERD, a posteriori beta 12-30 Hz) 150-600 ms post-stimulus at five midline clusters during a visual semantic Go/NoGo task, plus a supporting neuropsychological battery
Method_Architecture: Repeated-measures general linear models (group x trial type) per electrode cluster in SPSS 26 on EEGLAB newtimef short-time Fourier ERSP with gain-model baseline correction; Bonferroni-corrected post hoc contrasts, Cohen's d and eta squared, independent-samples t-test for Go RT, plus Bayes-factor confirmation of the behavioural nulls; no machine learning
Best_Metric: d = 1.155 (Cohen's d, central-cluster theta ERS on Go trials, LMCI > EMCI, p = .002); largest effect d = 1.581 (within-EMCI NoGo > Go theta); omnibus group x trial interaction F(1,33) = 23.76, p < .001, eta squared = .419 (no AUC)
Dataset: Local convenience sample - pre-training EEG from a subset of a pilot reasoning-training RCT (Mudar et al., 2019); IRB approval University of Texas at Dallas and UT Southwestern Medical Center; not a public dataset, available on request
Key_Novelty: First ERSP Go/NoGo comparison of EMCI vs LMCI theta ERS and alpha ERD
Primary_Limitation: Small cross-sectional sample (18 vs 17) with no cognitively normal control arm, single-subtest staging and unmodelled sex imbalance
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** whether the flattened Go/NoGo differentiation in LMCI reflects raised tonic inhibition, reduced attentional allocation or both; whether these ERSP markers track conversion longitudinally; whether they survive multi-domain rather than single-subtest staging. - **Applications:** low-cost EEG staging support for aMCI, trial stratification, pre/post intervention outcome measure. - **Methodologies:** resting-state versus task contrasts, longitudinal event-related EEG, wavelet or multitaper decomposition for beta, planned ERSP-behaviour association analyses.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 416 (2022), article number 113539; Elsevier B.V.

Modality: EEG/ERP electrophysiology - 64-channel NeuroScan SynAmps2 event-related potentials (P100, N1, N2, P300 and a four-window late positive potential spanning 500-5000 ms) during a description-based IAPS cognitive-reappraisal task, with sLORETA source localisation, Self-Assessment Manikin valence/arousal ratings and a full neuropsychological battery; CT or MRI for screening only
Method_Architecture: Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (Group x Condition) with Greenhouse-Geisser correction, Bonferroni post hoc and partial eta squared; independent t-tests on (Rea minus Neg) difference scores; Pearson/Spearman correlation in SPSS 22.0; sLORETA voxelwise randomisation testing (5000 permutations)
Best_Metric: r = -0.39 (Pearson, arousal reduction (Rea minus Neg) vs verbal fluency within the aMCI group, p 0.007); headline group contrast t = 3.205 (p 0.002) for smaller arousal down-regulation in aMCI, key neural effect LPP window-4 Condition x Group F(2,182) = 4.494 (p 0.020, partial eta squared 0.047) (no AUC)
Dataset: Locally collected single-centre clinical EEG/ERP dataset - Department of Neurology and Memory Clinic, Shanghai Tongji Hospital (aMCI) plus community-recruited healthy elderly controls, all Chinese aged 55-85; stimuli from the public IAPS set; not a public dataset
Sample_N_Approx: 93 (46 amnestic MCI / 47 healthy elderly controls; 72 aMCI and 50 HEC recruited, 26 aMCI and 3 HEC excluded)
Key_Novelty: First ERP study of cognitive reappraisal in amnestic MCI; late-window LPP marks reappraisal failure
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional single-centre design with one regulation strategy and no follow-up, so the early-detection biomarker claim is untested; compounded by asymmetric attrition (26 of 72 aMCI versus 3 of 50 HEC), modest effect sizes (partial eta squared 0.045-0.047, all correlations 0.39 or below) and decisive contrasts at the significance boundary (p 0.048, p 0.091).
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether late-window LPP and parietal source deficits predict MCI-to-dementia conversion (no longitudinal design); why no prefrontal group difference emerged; why hypoactivation was left-lateralised; whether the pooled-only LPP-arousal correlation is a power artefact. - **Applications:** Late LPP (Rea minus Neg) and sLORETA parietal current density as candidate aMCI biomarkers; emotion-regulation screening; cheaper regulation strategies for therapy. - **Methodologies:** Description-preceded IAPS reappraisal, REST re-referencing, four-window LPP, sLORETA permutation testing.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 427 (2022), article number 113800; Elsevier B.V.

Modality: Cerebral [18F]FDG-PET analysed voxelwise in SPM plus 18F-Florbetaben/18F-Flutemetamol amyloid PET, with CSF Abeta1-42, Abeta42/40, t-tau and p-tau, APOE genotyping, informant-rated IRI, Ekman-60 Faces Test and a full neuropsychological battery
Method_Architecture: One-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc, Wilcoxon signed-rank within-patient tests, chi-square, Bonferroni-corrected Spearman correlation, multiple linear regression and MANCOVA; voxelwise SPM multiple regression with age and MMSE as nuisance variables (p < 0.001 uncorrected, 50-voxel extent)
Best_Metric: r = -0.508 (Spearman rho, PD-T1 vs Category Fluency in the whole sample, p < 0.001, Bonferroni threshold p < 0.002); largest within-patient effect PD in AD 16.13 +/- 4.94 to 26.46 +/- 6.07 (Wilcoxon z = 5.76, p < 0.001) (no AUC)
Dataset: Single-centre memory-clinic cohort, University of Florence and Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria Careggi, Florence, Italy (FDG-PET and amyloid PET at the Careggi Nuclear Medicine Unit); not a public dataset
Sample_N_Approx: 111 (24 SCD / 41 MCI / 46 AD; 72 female / 39 male; imaging subsample 42 amyloid-positive: 24 AD / 18 MCI)
Key_Novelty: First FDG-PET metabolic correlates of empathy loss across the SCD-MCI-AD continuum
Primary_Limitation: No metabolic arm in the preclinical SCD group and no multiple-comparison correction voxelwise; the pre-onset empathy baseline is retrospective informant recall.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether rising emotional contagion predicts AD-driven decline; why PD rose in amyloid-negative as well as amyloid-positive MCI; why PD moved inversely with diagnosis, against Sturm 2013; why the EK-60 F group effect vanished under MANCOVA; why FT-T1 had no metabolic correlate. - **Applications:** FDG-PET for diagnosing socio-emotional deficits; informant-rated PD as a preclinical signal in SCD. - **Methodologies:** Dual retrospective/current informant IRI; SPM restricted to amyloid-positive patients; Bonferroni-thresholded Spearman screening, regression, MANCOVA.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 428 (2022), article number 113893; Elsevier B.V. (Editor's Choice)

Modality: Clinical neuropsychology - extended Uniform Data Set 3 battery (MoCA, Craft Story, RAVLT, Benson figure, MINT, verbal fluency, Digit Span, TMT-A/B, Digit Symbol, FAB, Stroop) plus HADS and trial-by-trial 64-item hand-administered WCST; no neuroimaging
Method_Architecture: Hierarchical Bayesian Attentional Learning Model (reward sensitivity r, punishment sensitivity p, decision consistency d) fitted in Stan to trial-by-trial WCST data with LOOIC model comparison, posterior predictive checks and parameter recovery; Bayesian t-tests/Mann-Whitney with Bayes factors, Kendall-rank correlations, maximum-likelihood factor analysis, elastic-net regression, bootstrapped mediation
Best_Metric: tau = 0.58 (Bayesian Kendall-rank correlation, Punishment Sensitivity vs WCST completed categories, [0.40, 0.72], BF10 > 100, p < 0.001); mirror reward association tau = -0.58 [-0.75, -0.41]; group contrast Punishment Sensitivity 0.003 vs 0.03, posterior difference -0.029, 95% HDI [-0.04, -0.006] (no AUC)
Dataset: Prospectively recruited single-centre clinical sample, Department of Cognitive Neurology, Neuropsychiatry and Neuropsychology, Fleni, Buenos Aires, Argentina; extended UDS3 battery but Fleni's own data, not NACC's; not publicly available (corresponding author on request)
Sample_N_Approx: 80 (42 aMCI: 24 single-domain / 18 multi-domain; 38 age-, sex- and education-matched controls)
Key_Novelty: First application of the Attentional Learning Model to WCST data in aMCI patients
Primary_Limitation: No neuroimaging was acquired, so the reward and punishment sensitivity parameters cannot be anchored to any brain network; the Reward Sensitivity group difference was inconclusive because its posterior HDI contained zero, and the 80-participant single-centre sample had no external validation and no non-amnestic MCI comparison group.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether altered reward/punishment sensitivity precedes, accompanies or follows memory decline; whether the parameters predict conversion to dementia; whether they generalise to non-amnestic MCI; whether the Reward Sensitivity elevation is real given its inconclusive posterior. - **Applications:** Intervention design (errorless learning, feedback scheduling) and stratification of aMCI by learning phenotype rather than domain count. - **Methodologies:** Hierarchical Bayesian modelling of trial-by-trial records from tests already in the clinical battery.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 471 (2024), article number 115099; Elsevier B.V. (Research article)

Modality: 3.0 T structural T1 MRI with FreeSurfer 7.2.0 surface-based morphometry (vertex-wise cortical thickness and surface area, Desikan-Killiany parcellation) plus T2 screening scan, a neuropsychological battery (MMSE, CDR, MoCA, WAIS-IV Digit Span, TMT A/B, modified Posner IOR-OT) and stopwatch-timed single- and dual-task Timed Up and Go
Method_Architecture: Covariate-adjusted vertex-wise general linear modelling in FreeSurfer (gender, age, total intracranial volume; 10 mm FWHM smoothing; Monte Carlo cluster correction), with chi-square, independent-samples t-tests, Mann-Whitney U and within-group partial Spearman correlation in SPSS 26.0; no machine learning
Best_Metric: r = 0.46 (Spearman rho, left superior parietal cortical thickness vs MoCA total in HC only, p 0.011); thickness vs DT-TUG time rho = -0.45 (p 0.013); group difference is a left superior parietal surface-area cluster (599.65 mm2, 1480 vertices, vertex p < 0.005, cluster p < 0.05) (no AUC)
Dataset: Single-centre cross-sectional clinical and community cohort, Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China (Oct 2021 - Sep 2022); not a public dataset, available on request from the corresponding author
Key_Novelty: Left superior parietal surface area links cognition and dual-task walking in MCI
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional design with only 30 per group cannot establish causality; every significant cortex-to-behaviour correlation occurred in controls only, and the within-HC positive surface-area to DT-TUG association runs opposite to the between-group finding of smaller surface area in MCI. Dozens of Spearman correlations appear uncorrected for multiple comparisons, power was calculated only for DT-TUG at 75 %, MoCA served as both diagnostic gatekeeper and outcome, and MCI was defined clinically with no biomarker confirmation or amnestic/non-amnestic subtyping.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether reduced left superior parietal surface area precedes or follows cognitive and dual-task decline; why the difference appeared in surface area but not thickness (speculative cortical stretching); why the effect was left-lateralised; why IOR-OT was prolonged without correlating with either cortical measure. - **Applications:** Dual-task TUG as a bedside MCI screen where single-task TUG failed; left superior parietal surface area as a candidate structural marker. - **Methodologies:** FreeSurfer 7.2.0 vertex-wise morphometry with Monte Carlo correction.
Journal: Behavioural Brain Research, volume 479 (2025), article number 115360; Elsevier B.V. (open access, CC BY-NC)

Modality: 3T diffusion tensor imaging (64 directions, b = 1000 s/mm2) with whole-brain TBSS FA skeleton and ICBM atlas-based ROI quantification of FA, MD, lambda1 and lambda23; T1 and T2 FLAIR for anatomy and lesion exclusion; metabolic bloods and a neuropsychological battery (MoCA, CDT, VFT, AVLT) as correlates
Method_Architecture: FSL/PANDA Tract-Based Spatial Statistics voxelwise three-group comparison on an FA skeleton (threshold 0.2, multiple-comparison corrected) plus atlas-based ROI FA/MD; t test, Mann-Whitney U, ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-squared/Fisher; Pearson correlation adjusted for age, gender and education
Best_Metric: TBSS voxel extent 6.02% (8302/137,832 skeleton voxels) with elevated MD and 4.38% (6045/137,832) with elevated lambda23 in MetS-MCI vs MetS-NC, P < 0.05 corrected; largest clinical contrast MoCA 21.86 +/- 2.00 vs 26.47 +/- 0.63 vs 26.53 +/- 0.56, P < 0.001 (no AUC)
Dataset: Single-centre cross-sectional clinical cohort, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China (MetS patients recruited February - November 2024); 3T GE Discovery MR750; not a public dataset
Key_Novelty: First DTI comparison of MetS with vs without MCI, linking myelin (lambda23) loss to cognition
Primary_Limitation: Small, single-centre, cross-sectional sample (36/30/38) that cannot establish causal ordering among metabolic syndrome, white matter degradation and MCI, and is too small to stratify by MetS severity or by individual metabolic component; compounded by the near-complete confounding of MetS status with hypertension (83.33% and 90.00%) and diabetes (55.56% and 73.33%) against a control group with zero prevalence of either, and by reporting of ROI diffusion values and correlation coefficients only in figures.
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether myelin sheath damage is an early biomarker of cognitive decline in MetS; the molecular mechanism linking metabolic dysregulation to myelin loss; whether the tract-to-domain associations (EC and IFO for executive function; EC, IFO and UF for memory) replicate in a broader population; why the left IFO spans more cognitive domains than the right. - **Applications:** lambda23 as a stratification or monitoring endpoint in metabolic intervention trials; tract-specific targets for early intervention. - **Methodologies:** Prospective longitudinal DTI with conversion outcomes, expanded samples permitting component-wise stratification, myelin-specific imaging or fluid myelin markers, and tractography-based rather than atlas-based ROI definition.

Modality: Behavioural cognitive-experimental protocol - laptop boundary extension task (15 s display, 35-minute filled delay, recall and cued generation drawings, four-variant recognition with confidence ratings) plus a full neuropsychological battery (WAIS-III, WMS-III LM-II/FP-II, WSLT-II, MMSE, BVRT, CTT, VNT, SAVF, JLO, GDS-15); plasma T-tau and P-tau by immunomagnetic reduction in a 12-participant subsample; structural MRI used only for exclusion and Scheltens medial temporal atrophy rating
Method_Architecture: Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc alpha 0.017 and effect size r, Mann-Whitney U, Spearman rho and education-controlled partial correlations; dual-process signal-detection ROC modelling (ROC Toolbox) of confidence-binned boundary judgements to estimate recollection, familiarity, da and B''; Matlab pixel-ratio object proportion scoring
Best_Metric: r = 0.42 (effect size for the significant YA vs MCI post hoc difference in ROC-derived familiarity; Kruskal-Wallis overall p = 0.002, medians 0.64 YA / 0.37 OA / -0.25 MCI); largest effect r = 0.48 for YA vs OA generation-phase object proportion (no AUC)
Dataset: Locally recruited Taiwanese cohort, not a public dataset - 80 community volunteers recruited by advertisement in Taichung plus 26 memory-clinic patients from National Taiwan University Hospital and Asia University Hospital; 20-photograph Intraub and Richardson (1989) stimulus set with five Taiwanese substitutions
Sample_N_Approx: 106 (40 younger adults / 40 healthy older adults / 26 MCI); plasma tau subsample 12 (9 OA / 3 MCI)
Key_Novelty: First use of boundary extension as a pure familiarity measure to separate MCI from healthy aging
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional preliminary design with only 26 clinic-recruited MCI patients, no conversion follow-up and no reported classification accuracy or AUC
Open_Problems: - **Open problems:** Whether reduced BE familiarity predicts MCI-to-AD conversion; why object proportion scores fail to separate OA from MCI while recognition familiarity does; whether the education-familiarity link reflects semantic knowledge or general reserve. - **Applications:** Low-cost laptop-and-drawing screening adjunct for lower-education cohorts; a reserve-assessment tool complementing standard batteries. - **Methodologies:** Longitudinal conversion endpoints, larger amyloid/tau PET or CSF arms, automated OP scoring, per-subject ROC fit diagnostics.
Journal: Archives of Gerontology and Geriatrics, volume 94 (2021), article 104329; Elsevier B.V.

Modality: Clinical neuropsychological outcome measures pooled from 7 cognitive-intervention trials - MMSE as the primary instrument, with DRS-2, ADAS-Cog, RBMT, RAVLT, COWAT and TMT among the domain tests; no imaging or fluid data
Method_Architecture: Systematic review under PRISMA (Moher et al., 2009), registered in PROSPERO as CRD42020189135. Five-database search (PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Collaborative Central Register
Best_Metric: MD = +0.3625 MMSE points (mean change from baseline in the cognitive-intervention arms against a mean decrease of 0.2213 points in controls, Wilcoxon test across the included trials)

Modality: Routine clinical work-up combining neuropsychological testing (MMSE and MoCA with its executive component), visual medial temporal atrophy grading on brain CT, and 18F-FDG-PET read as suggestive or not suggestive of Alzheimer dementia
Method_Architecture: Retrospective consecutive-sampling cohort design with one-year clinical follow-up in a single geriatric memory clinic. Standardised neuropsychological battery: MMSE (Folstein et al
Best_Metric: AUC 0.873 (95% CI 0.800-0.946) for the full multivariable model; the 2-step procedure achieves Acc 81.1% (95% CI 74.7-87.5), sensitivity 71.0%, specificity 83.9%
Dataset: Single-centre retrospective outpatient cohort, Geriatrics Unit, S. Orsola-Malpighi Hospital, University of Bologna, Italy

Primary_Limitation: The primary limitation is author-stated and concerns the absence of the evidence that would confirm the endpoint was real: "AD neuropathologic biomarkers were not prospectively collected in the trial." Every one of the 96 adjudicated endpoint events therefore rests on clinical determination alone, with no pathological confirmation that the participants adjudicated as having MCI due to AD had Alzheimer's pathology rather than another cause of impairment - which matters especially here, since the committee's kappa against site investigators was only 0.327 for that determination, so the clinical
Open_Problems: Whether the participants repeatedly triggered and repeatedly judged not to meet MCI criteria would eventually have met them is explicitly left unresolved: "it remains unknown whether they would have been given such a diagnosis had they been observed for longer durations." That is a question about whether the committee's conservatism produced false negatives, and only longer follow-up can answer it. Whether behavioural and psychiatric symptom scales would improve early detection is nominated as untested. The broader open problem is whether the MCI due to AD construct can be operationalised reli
Journal: The Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease (JPAD), published by Serdi. The citation line prints "J Prev Alz Dis 20

Modality: Clinical Frameworks and Population Studies (EHR/surveys/neuropsych/cohorts/epidemiology). This is a community cohort study whose data are interview responses, self-reported sociodemographic and health history, clinic measurements and a neuropsychological battery, analysed epidemiologically. C3 is the rival that must be rejected
Method_Architecture: Community-based participatory recruitment through door-to-door solicitation, flyers, community events, churches and food banks in four rural counties, with bilingual interviewing;
Best_Metric: OR 2.98 (95% CI: 1.72-5.15), high excess predicted heart/vascular age vs MCI at baseline, fully adjusted
Dataset: Project FRONTIER (Facing Rural Obstacles to healthcare Now Through Intervention, Education & Research), an ongoing community-based participatory cohort study of chronic disease and cognitive aging in a multi-ethnic rural population, run from the Garr
Sample_N_Approx: 967 - 340 without HEPHA/627 with HEPHA (238 in the 3-year follow-up analysis)
Key_Novelty: First study relating predicted heart/vascular age to MCI in a rural multiethnic cohort
Primary_Limitation: The primary limitation is author-stated and is a generalisability limitation: "The primary limitation of this study is that the sample were obtained from a geographically limited area and therefore the findings of this study may or may not be generalizable to other rural communities in the U.S." Four adjacent counties in West Texas, all below national and state per-capita income, with a sample that is 64% Hispanic and only 2% non-Hispanic Black, is a narrow base from which to generalise to rural America, and the authors say so directly. Open_Problems: Whether changing PHA changes cognitive trajectory is the open question this study raises without answering, and the authors specify the trial design that would answer it - randomising participants to app-based PHA feedback against conventional risk communication, with cognitive outcomes. The broader unresolved issue they name is that "evidence for change in PHA or changes in individual CVD risk burden influencing future cognitive function is limited". The window they argue for intervention is young adulthood and midlife, consistent with their cohort's mean age of 55. Whether PHA outperforms it
Journal: The Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease (JPAD), published by Serdi, with the copyright line reading "Serdi and

Modality: Computerised cognitive battery (Cogstate CBB + ISLT) with PiB-PET-defined amyloid groups
Method_Architecture: Linear mixed models (R lme4/lmerTest), Cohen d effect sizes
Best_Metric: Not reported - no classification metric; ISLT total decline d=0.93 (Abeta+ MCI vs CN, 18 mo), d=0.91 delayed
Dataset: AIBL (AIBL-ROCS substudy)
Sample_N_Approx: 98 - 67 Abeta- CN / 16 Abeta+ MCI / 15 Abeta+ mild AD
Key_Novelty: Frequent 3-monthly Cogstate/ISLT testing detects decline in small Abeta+ MCI/AD samples
Primary_Limitation: Very small Abeta+ MCI and AD groups (n<20), no multiple-comparison correction, practice effects likely obscured visual/working-memory decline; industry-funded analysis.
Open_Problems: Whether quarterly ISLT/CBB assessment reduces trial sample sizes needs a formal power demonstration; larger samples, longer follow-up and APOE covariance analyses required.
Journal: The Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease (JPAD)

Modality: Bibliometric analysis of VR cognitive assessment/intervention literature
Method_Architecture: CiteSpace 5.7 R3 bibliometric networks, co-citation clustering
Best_Metric: Not reported - bibliometric study; no classification metric
Dataset: Web of Science Core Collection
Key_Novelty: First CiteSpace bibliometric visualisation of VR research in MCI (1995-2020, 230 records)
Primary_Limitation: Single-database (Web of Science) bibliometric analysis ending 2020, so rankings are incomplete and post-2020 growth is unrepresented.
Open_Problems: Post-2020 VR-MCI growth uncaptured; bibliometric indicators measure attention not effectiveness; VR technology suitable for the elderly still underdeveloped.

Modality: Olfactory identification (BSIT) longitudinal trajectories with autopsy neuropathology
Method_Architecture: Linear mixed models, backward timescale, multiple imputation (SAS)
Best_Metric: Not reported - trajectory study; MCI-by-time beta=-0.09 (-0.13,-0.05), dementia beta=-0.19
Dataset: Rush Memory and Aging Project (MAP)
Sample_N_Approx: 900 cognitively intact (289 incident MCI / 610 stable), from 1318; 239 dementia sub-analysis; 334 autopsy
Key_Novelty: Backward-timescale BSIT trajectories diverge 5 years pre-MCI and 3 years pre-dementia
Primary_Limitation: Autopsy subsample was older, more impaired and less representative; olfaction testing began 2011 despite 1997 enrolment; single 12-point BSIT instrument.
Open_Problems: Whether olfactory-trajectory monitoring is operationalisable as screening, and whether intervention at rapid-decline point prevents progression, remain open; non-AD pathology drivers unresolved.

Modality: Tactile (von Frey QST), visual (FrACT) and auditory (audiometry) sensory thresholds
Method_Architecture: Ranked-data ANCOVA with covariates, Spearman correlations (SPSS)
Best_Metric: Not reported - no classification metric; tactile group effect eta2=0.18, rs=0.39 (memory)
Dataset: Baseline of two interventional RCTs (Mannheim MCI + frailty) plus NCC recruitment
Key_Novelty: MCI vs frailty vs control sensory study isolating tactile (not visual/auditory) loss in MCI
Primary_Limitation: Cross-sectional with a small, trial-derived MCI sample (n=31); single-finger mechanical threshold; directionality untestable.
Open_Problems: Prospective validation of tactile sensitivity as an MCI predictor, whether multimodal sensory assessment improves stratification, and whether sensorimotor training improves cognition.

Modality: Serious games (digital health) protocol with MMSE/ACE-R validation anchors
Method_Architecture: Protocol: PRISMA review, expert focus group, Unity 3D, planned ML
Best_Metric: Not reported - protocol only, no results
Dataset: Not applicable (protocol; planned Iran recruitment)
Key_Novelty: Protocol for MMSE/ACE-R-mapped serious games for MCI diagnosis and training in Persian
Primary_Limitation: Protocol only with no results; before-after design cannot separate game effects from practice; MoCA/mini-Cog anchors excluded for staffing reasons.
Open_Problems: Whether game scores correlate sufficiently with MMSE/ACE-R for diagnosis, whether repeated play improves cognition, and the diagnostic value of machine-learning scoring of game behaviour.

Modality: Meta-analysis of EVOO dietary-intervention RCTs with cognitive scale outcomes
Method_Architecture: Random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird), GRADE, R Meta package
Best_Metric: SMD 0.29 (95% CI 0.18-0.41) overall; MMSE MD 0.42, CDT MD 0.47, ADAS-Cog MD 1.45
Dataset: 5 RCTs (Italy, Greece, Spain, USA; incl. PREDIMED)
Key_Novelty: First EVOO RCT meta-analysis in MCI/dementia; significant but below MCID thresholds
Primary_Limitation: Only 5 RCTs with low-moderate GRADE certainty; pooled effects below MCID; significance depends partly on the two PREDIMED trials.
Open_Problems: Larger standardised-dosing EVOO RCTs, MCI-vs-dementia stratum separation, and dose-response via uniform polyphenol reporting; clinical significance remains unproven.

Modality: Olfactory identification (DESK 20-item kit, 10 odorants x 2 concentrations)
Method_Architecture: Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman, ROC analysis, standardised regression (SAS)
Best_Metric: AUC 0.766 (healthy vs MCI, 3 strong odorants); 0.953 (healthy vs AD); 0.810 (MCI vs AD)
Dataset: Multicenter Japan (5 facilities; UMIN000041794)
Key_Novelty: Japanese-designed DESK olfactory kit (10 familiar odorants) discriminates HC/MCI/AD; AUC up to 0.953
Primary_Limitation: Age effect on DESK scores not fully explored given large inter-group age differences; open-label design and sponsor-developed tool.
Open_Problems: Age-stratified DESK norms, longitudinal predictive value, optimal odorant subset, and independent non-sponsor validation.

Modality: Nutritional intervention RCT (grape seed procyanidins 320 mg/d) with MoCA outcome
Method_Architecture: Mixed-design ANOVA, paired t-tests (SPSS 16.0)
Best_Metric: Not reported - MoCA change 2.35 vs 1.28; mean difference 1.06 (95% CI -0.55 to 2.68), P=0.192
Dataset: Community cohort Huangshi City, Hubei, China (ChiCTR-IPR-16008164)
Key_Novelty: First RCT of grape seed procyanidin extract (320 mg/d, 6 mo) in elderly MCI; null
Primary_Limitation: Underpowered (81% power for 0.6 SD effect) with 25.7% intervention-arm dropout; MoCA-only outcome and no baseline diet survey.
Open_Problems: Procyanidin monomer vs oligomer/polymer forms, longer duration and larger samples, subgroup benefit analysis, and biochemical adherence markers.

Modality: Structural MRI (3D-T1) individual gray matter networks (KLS, Schaefer-400)
Method_Architecture: SVM (LIBSVM/scikit-learn) with BrainSpace gradient + Gretna topology
Best_Metric: bACC 79.4% (Sens 81.7% / Spec 77.1%)
Dataset: ADNI
Key_Novelty: First MCI-converter discrimination via individual GM-network gradient compression; SVM bACC 79.4%
Primary_Limitation: ADNI-only with no external validation; first-of-kind finding requiring replication; 79.4% balanced accuracy below clinical grade.
Open_Problems: External replication, structural+functional connectome fusion, multi-atlas robustness, and longitudinal development of gradient compression.

Modality: Narrative review of tactile discrimination testing in MCI/AD
Method_Architecture: Narrative literature synthesis (4 databases, 146 records)
Best_Metric: Not reported - narrative review; no classification metric
Dataset: Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, Google Scholar literature
Key_Novelty: Narrative review positioning tactile discrimination as an MCI diagnostic indicator
Primary_Limitation: Narrative (non-systematic) review; the claim of superior accuracy vs visual/auditory tasks is unquantified; animal evidence unweighted.
Open_Problems: Standardised tactile protocol and norms, longitudinal predictive validity, head-to-head tactile vs visual/auditory accuracy, and sensory-training intervention effects.

Modality: CHARLS 2015 national ageing survey: telephone cognition battery (31-point HRS-style), CESD-10, self-reported sleep duration and leisure activity, handgrip dynamometry, gait speed, FTSST, anthropometric ASM, WBC/CRP
Method_Architecture: Logistic regression with 17-covariate adjustment plus bootstrap mediation and moderated-mediation (conditional indirect effect) models in SPSS 26.0 with PROCESS v4.2
Best_Metric: OR 1.781 (95% CI 1.331-2.385) for sleep 4 h or less, fully adjusted; no Acc/AUC/F1 reported
Dataset: CHARLS 2015 wave (China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study)
Key_Novelty: Sleep duration and leisure activity indirectly moderate the depression-sarcopenia-MCI mediation
